title: Sustainable Supply Chain Management
text:
What you will learn
This online script is your guide through the readings, tests and exercises that we will do in this course.
Topics: productivity · process strategy and capacity · design for sustainability · quality · forecasting · supply chains · sales and operations planning

title: Sustainable Supply Chain Management
text:
The title in two pictures
Supply chain — the firms and steps from raw material to customer. Materials move forward, orders and information move back.



A beer supply chain. Materials move forward (red), orders and information move backward (magenta). Own illustration.


Sustainable — profit drives a firm, but it also causes effects it does not pay for (external effects, Latin externus, “outward”). In this module: the environmental effects — CO₂, energy, materials, waste — beside profit. A definition is a tool, like a flashlight: it lights one part of the room sharply.



The firm, driven by profit, and its external effects. The module’s definition puts the flashlight on the environmental ones. Own illustration.

title: Week 1 — Operations and productivity
text:
Key content
Download as text · quiz-me prompt · exercises


Problem
Every service is a small production: inputs (people, equipment, organisation) → output.
Operations = the part of a firm that turns inputs into outputs. Productivity = output ÷ input.


Sentence of the week
Productivity is always a ratio, and the interesting question is what goes into the denominator.
Numerator (output): easy to count. Denominator (input): a choice that decides the answer. No input named → no meaning.


Formulas








Measure
In words
Unit, e.g.




Productivity
output ÷ input
guests per person-hour


Single-factor
output ÷ one input
crates per labor-hour, units per kWh


Multifactor
output ÷ all inputs, in money
titles per dollar, units per euro


Growth
(new − old) ÷ old
%




Person-hour = labor-hour = one person, one hour
Multifactor: convert every input to money first (hours + kg + kWh cannot be added)
Growth: always divide by the old value
Heizer et al. (2023), Ch. 1: The productivity challenge, Productivity measurement



Student life

Party, 20 guests: 335 person-minutes = 5.58 person-hours → 20 ÷ 5.58 = 3.58 guests per person-hour; per euro of food: a second, different productivity
Mia’s moving day: output fixed (100 moving units); inputs vary (van size, crew, pizza) → units per person-hour vs. units per euro can rank the plans differently



Factory: textbook anchors

Collins Title: 8 titles ÷ 32 labor-hours = 0.25 → new system 14 ÷ 32 = 0.4375, +75 %; multifactor 8 ÷ 1,040 $ = 0.0077 → 14 ÷ 1,440 $ = 0.0097, +26 %. Same change, two measures, two gains
Modern Lumber (Solved Problems 1.1, 1.2): 240 crates ÷ 300 labor-hours = 0.800 → 260 ÷ 308 = 0.844, +5.5 %; multifactor 240 ÷ 4,500 $ = 0.0533 → 260 ÷ 4,580 $ = 0.0568, +6.4 %
Fisher Technologies (Table 1.1): contribution 10,500 $; sales +50 % → 18,000 $; finance costs −50 % → 12,750 $; production costs −20 % → 22,500 $. Operations = strongest lever



Supply chain
Output = products delivered to customers; input = what all firms spend (€) or emit (t CO₂). One firm’s gain can be the chain’s loss; € and CO₂ can point in opposite directions.


Productivity variables

Labor — people, skills, health
Capital — equipment, tools
Management — organisation, technology, knowledge (find in the chapter which one contributes most to growth)
Services: output hard to count; quality escapes the count



Typical errors

No unit (“3.6” says nothing)
Adding hours, kg and kWh — convert to money first
Growth divided by the new value (43 % instead of +75 %)
Faster ≠ more productive (more people can lower output per person-hour)
Ranking ratios with different denominators against each other



Practice items (no keys)

Copy shop: 1,200 pages, 2 people × 6 h → new printer: 1,500 pages, same staff. Pages per labor-hour before/after? Growth in %?
Food truck: 240 wraps; 2 workers × 10 h × 15 €, ingredients 360 €, fuel and gas 40 €, rent 100 €. Wraps per euro? Which input to cut first, and why?
Cargo bike 80 parcels/day vs. van 120 parcels/day: two denominators favouring the bike, one favouring the van.

title: Week 2 — Process strategy and capacity
text:
Key content
Download as text · quiz-me prompt


Problem
At 12:15 the Mensa queue reaches the door, yet the cashier waits half the time. The main-dish counter serves 120 guests an hour, the cashier 240, and 180 arrive: the queue grows by 60 guests an hour in front of the counter. A second cashier changes nothing.
Warm-up (role play): six departments of a bike company, each defending its own single-factor number, face a rush order of 2,000 bikes in four weeks. That is 500 bikes a week: whose capacity decides whether it fits?


Sentence of the week
A process can only go as fast as its slowest step, and that step sets the output for everyone.


Formulas in words








Measure
In words
Unit, e.g.




Capacity of a step
60 min ÷ minutes per unit × parallel workers or machines
pizzas per hour


Batch machine
units per load × 60 ÷ minutes per load
rolls per hour


Bottleneck
the step with the lowest capacity
—


Line capacity
capacity of the bottleneck
pizzas per hour


Bottleneck time
minutes per unit at the bottleneck
min per pizza


Throughput time
sum of all step times of one unit, no waiting
min


Utilization
actual output ÷ design capacity
%


Efficiency
actual output ÷ effective capacity
%


Break-even volume
fixed cost ÷ (price − variable cost per unit)
units per year


Crossover volume
difference in fixed cost ÷ difference in variable cost
units per year




Design capacity = the most in ideal conditions; effective capacity = with planned losses (set-ups, cleaning, breaks, product mix); actual output = what was really made
People and machines: always round up
Heizer et al. (2023), Ch. 7 Process strategy and Supplement 7 Capacity and constraint management



Student life

Party pizza line: dough 3 min, toppings 4 min, oven 10 min for 2 pizzas, cut 2 min → capacities 20 / 15 / 12 / 30 per hour → the oven is the bottleneck, 12 pizzas per hour. One pizza needs 19 min from dough to plate; 24 pizzas take 19 + 23 × 5 = 134 min
A second topper changes nothing. A second oven makes 24 per hour possible → the toppings become the bottleneck (15 per hour): the bottleneck moves
Moving day: the narrow staircase, not the size of the van



Factory

Every step of a line can be busy or idle; only the bottleneck decides the output. More people at a non-bottleneck step add cost, not output
Process strategies by volume and variety: process focus (low volume, high variety: job shop, craft bakery), repetitive focus (modules on a line: sandwich or roll line), product focus (high volume, low variety: continuous flow), mass customization (high volume and high variety)
Crossover chart: a process with high fixed and low variable cost wins above the crossover volume



Supply chain
A chain delivers only what its weakest firm delivers. Frames 400, assembly 500, distribution 600 bikes per week → 400 bikes per week. Expanding a firm that is not the bottleneck adds cost, not deliveries.


Typical errors

Adding the capacities of the steps instead of taking the minimum
Utilization and efficiency swapped: utilization divides by design, efficiency by effective capacity
Adding people at a step that is not the bottleneck
Forgetting parallel machines or the batch size of the oven
Throughput time (one unit, all steps) confused with bottleneck time (time between two finished units)

title: Week 1 exercises
text:
Part A · Problems from the textbook
Test 1 (next Thursday, 09:00) has calculation items of exactly the kinds below, with changed numbers, plus questions on the Frito-Lay and Hard Rock Cafe cases at the end of Chapter 1. Work on paper, with a calculator; write the unit next to every result.
The formulas in words. Productivity = output ÷ input. Single-factor productivity = output ÷ one input (labor-hours, kWh, kg). Multifactor productivity = output ÷ all inputs in money (hours, kilograms and kWh cannot be added; euros can). Productivity growth = (new − old) ÷ old.
Start here: Solved Problems 1.1 and 1.2 (Modern Lumber) at the end of Chapter 1, then the Collins Title examples in the chapter text. The Week 1 key content walks through all three.
Solve these from Chapter 1 of Heizer et al. (2023). The problem texts are in the book. ● = warm-up, ●● = test level, ●●● = stretch. Do at least the ● and ●● problems.

The in-class bonus
In Weeks 1–6 the afternoon ends with a bonus sheet: four to six items, done alone, on paper, in class, with your code name at the top. You scan it with your phone and upload it to ILIAS by 15:30. It counts if every item is attempted with the calculation path visible and more than half of the results are correct, and it improves your grade on the next test by 0.3 (for example from 2.3 to 2.0), if that test is passed. The bonus sheet is handed out in class only; it is never on this site. The exercises on this page are the training for it. Details: Assessment.

text:
Peer evaluation
Fink’s method (O’Dwyer, 2020):

100 points per student, distributed among the other members of your team, by contribution; equal points are allowed
Peer score = the points you receive from your teammates; with equal points it is 100
Your multiplier = peer score ÷ 100, applied to your team-test and group-project marks
Example: team mark 80, peer score 95 → 80 × 0.95 = 76; peer score 105 → 80 × 1.05 = 84
Your points change your teammates’ grades: give them with care





Michaelsen, L. K., Knight, A. B., & Fink, L. D. (Eds.). (2004). Team-based learning: A transformative use of small groups in college teaching. Stylus.

title: Group project
text:
The task
Your group picks one real product, builds a small dataset for its factory line and its key supplier, and simulates in Google Colab what a supply-chain disruption does to the line and how one countermeasure helps. You show the result as an animation and a poster at the poster session on Thursday 12 November.
Every project answers one question: When our key supplier fails, what happens to units per week, cost per unit and CO₂ per unit, and what should we do about it?

title: Group project
text:
Item
Rule

title: Group project
text:
Choosing your product
Choose a product you care about, as long as its factory works like the bike factory. Your product must meet four rules:

It is a physical product assembled from parts, made in 4–6 steps (stations) on one line.
It has one key purchased component with at least two real sourcing options, for example a cheap supplier far away and a dearer one close by.
It is sold in Europe, so you can find at least its price in public.
Each product appears once in the class. First registration wins.

Not allowed: food, drinks and chemicals (they flow through tanks, not stations), services and software.
The table shows the kind of product that fits. The sourcing options are illustrations; you research your own.

title: Group project
text:
What you build
You hand in four things: a dataset, a model notebook, an animation and a poster. Each one feeds the next.

1. Dataset pack
Your data uses the same files and column names as the UrbanRide bike data, so the course tools and the check cell run on it unchanged. Open the UrbanRide bike data (online with Week 2) first: its twelve tables, README and data dictionary are your worked example.








File
One row per
Columns

product_id, component_id, component_name, qty_per_unit, mass_kg, unit_cost_eur, supplier_id, added_at_workcenter

You may reuse three bike files unchanged: transport_modes.csv, transport_emission_factors.csv and the electricity row of emission_factors.csv. Every other number you type in needs a row in sources.csv. Its source_type is one of three: public (a figure with a link), analogy (a bike value adapted, with the reason) or guesstimate (your own estimate with the calculation shown, for example a station time you stopped on a factory video).


2. Model notebook
One Colab notebook simulates one year (52 weeks) of your line fed by your key supplier. It runs three scenarios, each with the 10 random seeds 1–10, and reports the mean and the lowest and highest value:

Baseline: normal operation.
Disruption: one supply-chain event, such as the supplier stopping for three weeks, the lead time doubling or a port closing. You back it with a real event of the same kind (a news report or a published case).
Disruption plus countermeasure: one response of your choice, such as safety stock, a second supplier, a nearer supplier, faster transport or a change on the line.

Each run fills the same scoreboard of four numbers: units per week; one-year total cost per unit; kg CO₂e per unit (key component, factory electricity and transport of the key component); and hours the line stood still for lack of parts.
The one-year total cost adds everything the year costs, including the CO₂ emitted:
\[
\text{Total cost} = \text{materials} + 52 \times \text{station fixed costs} + \text{transport} + 0.20 \times \text{average inventory value} + 100 \,\tfrac{\text{EUR}}{\text{t}} \times \text{t CO}_2\text{e}
\]
The 20 % inventory holding rate and the price of 100 EUR per tonne CO₂e are course values, the same for every group. Cost per unit is the total cost divided by the units made in the year.


3. Animation
The animation shows your line (stations, queues, parts waiting) and your supply chain (supplier, transport, stock of the key component) moving through time. You receive a template in Week 4. Your notebook writes its results into a file called results.json; the template reads that file and plays inside a Colab cell, and you save it as animation.html.
You may restyle the template or rebuild it in D3, but its numbers must come from results.json. The viewer must be able to switch between baseline, disruption and countermeasure.


4. Poster and appendix
One A1 portrait poster tells your answer in this order: the question, your product and line in one figure, the disruption and the real event behind it, the scoreboard for all three scenarios, and the course idea that explains each result (bottleneck, variability and waiting, Little’s Law, lead time and safety stock, total cost against unit price, CO₂ per unit).
The poster rests on two peer-reviewed journal articles as sources for the course ideas it uses, cited in APA with DOI. Textbooks, websites and AI answers do not count. Suitable journals include the Journal of Operations Management, Journal of Supply Chain Management, Journal of Business Logistics, Production and Operations Management, Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management, and Supply Chain Management: An International Journal; other journals need approval at the checkpoint. Every member must be able to explain each paper’s key argument: the question it asks, what it finds, and why that explains one of your results.
A two-page appendix holds your sources.csv as a table, the printed output of the check cell, the key argument of each paper in three sentences in your own words, and your AI note.

title: Group project
text:
The check cell
Your notebook must pass five tests that a fixed, read-only check cell runs on your files and your baseline results. You receive the cell in Week 4. Copy it into your notebook unchanged: the grader runs the original on your files, so an edited copy gains you nothing.








Test
Passes when
Why it matters




T1 Format
Every required file exists with the exact column names; no value is missing or negative
The course tools read your data like the bike data


T2 Capacity
Every station is busy less than 100 % of its available time in the baseline
A line loaded over 100 % never reaches a steady state


T3 Little’s Law
Average parts on the line equal units per hour × average hours on the line, within 10 %
A model that breaks Little’s Law is counting wrong


T4 Flow balance
Units finished never exceed units started; key components used equal units finished × quantity per unit
Nothing appears from nowhere


T5 Margin
Baseline cost per unit is below the list price
A company that loses money on every unit in normal times is not plausible



The cell prints PASS or FAIL for each test. All five must pass at the checkpoint and at the final submission. A test passes on real data or it fails; there is no partial pass.

title: Group project
section: The poster session: where you show it is your work
text:
The poster session: where you show it is your work
You build the project at home, with any help you like, including AI. The poster session on Thursday 12 November is where you show that every member understands what the group built. Each group has 25 minutes at its poster:

Pitch, 5 minutes. The group presents the question, the answer and the scoreboard.
Individual questions, 15 minutes. Every member answers two questions alone, drawn by the examiner from three kinds; members may not hand a question to someone else.

A number: “Where does this station time in your sources.csv come from? What happens to the scoreboard if it is 20 % higher?”
The model: “Why does the queue build at this station? Why did your countermeasure cost what it cost?”
A paper: “What is the key argument of this paper, and which of your results does it explain?”

Live change, 5 minutes. The examiner changes one number in your data. Before the rerun, the group predicts which way each scoreboard number moves and why. Then you run the notebook and compare.

The whole group is responsible for every member’s understanding. Each question a member cannot answer soundly lowers the group’s score in part D, so the group mark rewards groups that explain their work to each other before the session. A wrong prediction in the live change costs little if the reasoning is sound; a right one with no reason earns little.

title: Group project
text:
Using AI
You may use AI for every part of the project: finding data, writing code, styling the animation, drafting the poster. Three rules keep the work yours:

An AI answer is not a source. A number an AI suggests enters sources.csv only after you trace it to a public figure or turn it into a guesstimate with your own calculation. The source type “AI” does not exist.
You can explain every line. Code you cannot explain in the poster session counts against you, however well it runs.
You write an AI note for the appendix, at most half a page: what you handed to AI, how you checked its output, and one AI mistake you found and how you found it.

title: Appendix A — Tools
text:
What Colab is
Google Colab is a notebook in your browser: text cells and code cells, and every code cell runs on a Google computer, not on yours. Think of a lab bench Google lends you for the afternoon: the tools are laid out, and when you leave, the bench is cleared. Your notebook stays on your Google Drive; the computer’s memory does not. A free Google account is enough; nothing to install.

Four steps, once per week

Open. Click Open … in Colab on the week page. (In class the notebook is also on ILIAS: download it, then File → Upload notebook.)
Save a copy. File → Save a copy in Drive. Work in your copy; the original stays clean.
Run the first code cell. It loads the tools. Warning “not written by Google”: click Run anyway.
Top to bottom. Every step ends with a check, ✅ or ❌. A ❌ comes with a hint: fix one line, run again.

title: Appendix A — Tools
text:
AI assistants
Allowed in every task. Two habits: predict the answer before you ask, and check the assistant’s number against one you computed by hand.

Academic Cloud — the service portal of German universities, run by GWDG (Göttingen). Sign in with your TH Köln account and use several language models in Chat AI, free of charge.
Prompts for this module — quiz-me prompt for revision with the week’s key content.
How to work with an assistant — AI Fluency: the four Ds, which model for which task, two applied examples.


Principles for GenAI in this programme

Support, not a substitute for thinking. Using GenAI to support your own work is welcome and recommended. It must not replace your own academic work.
Be able to explain it yourself. At any time, you must be able to explain your own work orally, on your own and in answer to follow-up questions.
Avoid your own work, and you fail. If central parts were not produced by you, the result is a fail (example: whoever cannot coherently explain a source or method more than twice has, as a rule, failed the examination).

Translated from the German original: Bartnik, R., & Haag, C. (2025). Rahmensetzung zur Nutzung generativer KI im Bachelor- und Master-Studiengang Wirtschaftsingenieurwesen (V02). TH Köln. PDF

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
text: After this page

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
text:
The model
AI Fluency is “the ability to work effectively, efficiently, ethically, and safely” with AI systems (Dakan & Feller, 2025). Rick Dakan (Ringling College of Art and Design) and Joseph Feller (University College Cork) break it into four competencies, the 4Ds: Delegation, Description, Discernment and Diligence. Anthropic teaches the framework in free courses, one of them for students (Dakan et al., 2025).
In this module we use the four Ds as four phases of one piece of work. You decide what to hand over, you describe it, you judge what comes back, and you vouch for the result. Description and Discernment form a loop: you describe, judge, describe again, until the output passes your check.





flowchart LR
  A["1 Delegation<br/>What goes to the AI?"] --> B["2 Description<br/>Say what you want"]
  B --> C["3 Discernment<br/>Is it right?"]
  C -- "not yet" --> B
  C -- "passes" --> D["4 Diligence<br/>Vouch for it"]


 The 4D cycle: Description and Discernment repeat until the output passes the check. 



Think of a head chef with a new kitchen assistant. The chef decides which jobs the assistant takes (Delegation), gives a clear order (Description), tastes the dish before it leaves the kitchen (Discernment), and answers to the guest for every plate (Diligence). The assistant is fast; the name on the menu is still the chef’s.

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
section: Three ways of working with AI
text:
Three ways of working with AI
The framework distinguishes three modes (Dakan & Feller, 2025). Delegation includes choosing among them.



Mode
What happens
Example in this module




Automation
The AI does a defined task on your instruction
“Turn this formula into a Python function”


Augmentation
You and the AI think and build together, step by step
Designing a productivity model for a new process


Agency
You set up an AI to act on its own, also for others
The quiz-me prompt: a tutor you configure once

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
section: Phase 1: Delegation — what goes to the AI?
text:
Phase 1: Delegation — what goes to the AI?
Decide before you open the chat. Three questions (Dakan & Feller, 2025):

Goal and task. What is the question? What answer would change a decision? Break the work into parts: yours, the AI’s, shared.
Platform. What can this assistant do, and what not? Can it run code? Does it see your file? Does it know the textbook’s numbers? (Usually not exactly.)
Task split. Hand over what is tedious and easy to check: code syntax, plots, formatting. Keep what needs judgement: the question, the formula in words, the expected answer, the interpretation.

Rule of thumb for this module: the formula in words and one hand-calculated result stay with you. Code, charts and layout can go to the AI.

Which model for which task
Models differ in speed and depth. A stronger model costs more time (and often money or quota); use it where reasoning matters.








Tier
Examples (autumn 2026)
Use it for




Fast
Gemini in Colab; “Flash”, “mini” or “Haiku” models; small models in Academic Cloud Chat AI
Explain one line, fix an error message, rename columns, change colours


Strong
Claude Sonnet, GPT-5, Gemini Pro (standard mode); the largest model in Chat AI
Write a function or a full block of cells, build a dashboard


Strong + thinking
The same models with thinking / reasoning switched on; Claude Opus
Plan a model’s structure, find a logic error, review someone’s code



Model names change every few months; the tiers stay. When in doubt: plan and review with the strongest model, type and fix with the fast one.

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
section: Phase 2: Description — say what you want
text:
Phase 2: Description — say what you want
The AI knows nothing about your task beyond what you write. Three kinds of description (Dakan & Feller, 2025):

Product description — what the result looks like: inputs with units, the formula in words, the output, the format (a Python function, a table, a chart), one example with the number you expect.
Process description — how to get there: one step at a time, not everything at once. “First the data, then the function, then a test, then the chart.”
Performance description — how the AI should behave: “Ask me before you assume a value.” “Explain each line in one comment.” “Use plain words for a first-year student.”

A good prompt carries context, task, constraints and a check:

Context. I study operations management. I model the productivity of a process in Google Colab with pandas. Task. Write a function labour_productivity(units, hours) that returns units per labour-hour. Constraints. Plain Python, one comment per line, no extra libraries. Check. With 120 units and 40 hours the result must be 3.0 units/hour. Add a test cell that prints ✅ if so.

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
text:
Phase 3: Discernment — is it right?
Judge the output; do not admire it. Three kinds of discernment (Dakan & Feller, 2025):

Product discernment — is the result correct and useful?

Matches your hand-calculated number?
Units right (per hour, not per shift)?
Change one input: does the output move in the direction you predicted?
Edge cases: zero hours, empty rows, negative values?

Process discernment — is the conversation working? Three rounds without progress → start a new chat with a better description, or switch to a stronger model.
Performance discernment — does a configured assistant (e.g. your quiz-me tutor) behave as intended? Does it wait for your answer, or give it away?

Typical AI errors in operations calculations: the code runs, the logic is wrong. Utilization computed against the wrong capacity; hours per shift multiplied twice; the bottleneck picked by processing time instead of load. Only your own number catches these.

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
text:
Phase 4: Diligence — vouch for it
You hand in the result; you answer for it (Bartnik & Haag, 2025; Dakan & Feller, 2025):

Creation diligence — no personal or confidential data in public tools. For data from a company or from fellow students, use Academic Cloud (servers in Germany) or anonymise first.
Transparency diligence — say what the AI did. In Colab: one markdown cell with the prompt, the model and what you changed.
Deployment diligence — before you hand it in or show it: every number checked, every line of code explainable by you. In this programme you must be able to explain your work orally at any time (see Tools → Principles).

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
text:
Applied example 1: a calculation model
Task. A productivity model in Colab: three process variants (e.g. moving day with 2, 3 or 4 helpers), labour productivity and multifactor productivity for each, one bar chart.








Phase
What to do
Model




1 Delegation
Write the question and both formulas in words on paper. Calculate one variant by hand. Mode: augmentation for the structure, automation for the code. Keep: formulas, hand result, interpretation. Hand over: code, table, chart.
—


2 Description
First prompt: ask for a model plan only (inputs, outputs, cells, no code). Then one prompt per cell: input table → function → test against your hand result → chart. Give units and your expected number in every prompt.
Plan: strong + thinking. Cells: strong, or Gemini in Colab for short cells


3 Discernment
Test cell prints ✅ for your hand-calculated variant. Predict the direction for one more helper, then run. Check units in the table header. Error message → paste it to the fast model with the cell. Result looks odd → ask a different strong model to review the function line by line.
Fixes: fast. Review: strong + thinking, different provider


4 Diligence
Markdown cell: prompts, model names, what you changed. Re-run the notebook top to bottom. Explain every line to a teammate without the AI.
—

title: Appendix B — AI Fluency
text:
Applied example 2: a dashboard
Task. A one-page dashboard from your model’s results: three KPI tiles (e.g. labour productivity, multifactor productivity, cost per unit), one chart comparing the variants, one filter or slider. Built in Colab with plotly, or as a single HTML file.








Phase
What to do
Model




1 Delegation
Decide on paper: who reads it, which decision it supports, which three KPIs, which chart. Sketch the layout by hand. Keep: KPI choice and definitions. Hand over: layout code, styling, interactivity.
—


2 Description
Give the column names, units and five sample rows, not the whole file. State the reader, the decision, each KPI with its formula in words, chart type, filter, and constraints (one file, no outside data, colour-blind-safe colours, axis titles with units). Ask for a text wireframe first, then the code. Afterwards change one thing per prompt.
Wireframe and first build: strong (long, coherent code). Small edits (labels, colours): fast


3 Discernment
Each KPI tile equals the number in your model’s table. Filter set to “all” gives the totals. Bars start at zero. Every axis has a title and unit. Ask the AI: “Explain how each KPI is computed” and compare with your definitions. Test with one extreme row.
Review of the code: strong + thinking


4 Diligence
Add source, date and “built with AI assistance (model, date)” to the dashboard footer. No personal data in the file. Be ready to explain each KPI and each chart choice.
—

title: Appendix C — Formula sheet
text:
Week 1 — productivity (Heizer Ch. 1)
Symbols are kept to the textbook’s; every line says in words what the formula does. The sheet grows by one block a week.
Source: Heizer et al. (2023), Ch. 1; moving-day rules from Handout 2 of Week 1.

title: Appendix C — Formula sheet
text:
Formula
In words
Units




Productivity = output ÷ input
how much comes out for each unit that goes in
guests per person-hour, crates per labor-hour


Single-factor productivity = output ÷ one input
one input at a time: labor-hours, kWh, kg of material
titles per labor-hour, units per kWh


Multifactor productivity = output ÷ (labor + material + energy + capital + other), all in money
all inputs at once; money is the only unit in which hours, kilograms and kWh can be added
titles per dollar, units per euro

title: Appendix E — Quiz-me prompt
text:
How to use this page
Why paste the key content? The assistant then quizzes you on our numbers and our wording — the party, the moving day, the textbook examples we calculated — instead of on a textbook it half remembers. The check is still yours: every worked example in the key content carries the number the assistant should arrive at.

title: Appendix E — Quiz-me prompt
text:
The prompt






Copy from here




Role. You are a revision tutor for the module Sustainable Supply Chain Management at TH Köln (Prof. Dr. Roman Bartnik). I am a Bachelor student in my first course taught in English, meeting operations management for the first time.
Material. Below this prompt I paste the key content of one week: the problem the chapter discusses, the sentence of the week, the formulas, examples from student life, the factory and the supply chain with their numbers, typical errors, and practice items without keys. Use only this material and the textbook chapter it names (Heizer, Render & Munson, Operations Management, 14th ed.). Do not invent numbers that are not in the material.
Method. Quiz me, one question at a time. Start with the problem in words, then the formula in words, then a calculation on one of the examples’ numbers with one value changed, then a practice item. After each of my answers: say whether it is right, show the calculation in at most four lines, and name the typical error I made if I made one. Never give the answer before I have tried. If I ask for the answer straight away, give one hint first.
Style. Plain words before the textbook term, every time: say output per one input and then (single-factor productivity). Short answers, at most six sentences, unless I ask for more. Units on every number. Where a formula appears, write it in words as well.
Test format. The real tests are on paper, individual then team, with calculation items on these numbers with changed values, and with recognition items on the chapter’s terms and cases. Mix both kinds. End the session with three items in the test’s format and a two-line summary of what I should reread.
Honesty. If the material does not contain what I ask, say so and point me to the chapter section named in it. Do not guess a number.

Key content of the week:
(paste here)

section: A follow-up prompt for the typical errors
text:
A follow-up prompt for the typical errors

Take the typical errors in the material. For each one, give me a short calculation that contains that error and ask me to find and fix it. Then show the corrected calculation in at most four lines.

The chapter. The assistant works from a page; the test draws on the chapter’s cases and terms as well as on the numbers. Read the chapter, then use the quiz.
